title: Personal Engineering Philosophy: Hard-Won Production Lessons
description: Neeraj shares opinionated, hard-won lessons from building production systems across backend, distributed, and cloud engineering work.
linkedin_post:
The most expensive lessons I've learned building production systems weren't about the wrong technology choice. They were about the wrong assumptions I held with too much confidence.

A few opinions I've formed over years of shipping Go backends, distributed services, and cloud-native systems:

**Simplicity is a discipline, not a default.** Complex systems don't start complex. They accumulate complexity through reasonable decisions made in isolation. The engineers I respect most are the ones who actively fight for simplicity even when the deadline is real and the clever solution is tempting.

**Premature abstraction is as dangerous as premature optimization.** I've seen more systems hurt by over-engineered interfaces than by tight coupling. Abstract when the pattern has actually repeated — not when you imagine it might.

**Operational cost is a first-class design concern.** How a system fails, how you debug it at 2am, how a new engineer can reason about it six months later — these aren't afterthoughts. They're part of the design surface. If you only evaluate tradeoffs at build time, you're missing half the problem.

**Strong opinions, loosely held — but hold them long enough to learn from them.** Changing your mind when new evidence arrives is good engineering. Abandoning your position every time someone pushes back is something else. The instinct to stand behind a technical decision, learn from its failure, and update your mental model is how judgment actually develops.

None of this is original. But there's a real difference between knowing these things and having them internalized through systems that broke in production.

What's one engineering principle you've had to earn the hard way?
